text: The Subcommittee on Higher Education and Workforce Development will come to order. I note that a quorum is present. Without objections, the chair is authorized to call a recess at any time. In today's workforce, the hiring process is costly and extremely inefficient. This is especially the case with employers who are searching for workers with needed, specialized skills. For workers, attempting to navigate the job market is now more complicated than ever. Translating skills gained through education, training, and life experience into terms that employers understand is daunting. In this present era of innovation, which now includes the power of AI, we need smarter ways to connect job seekers' skills with employers' needs. Our economy is changing dramatically, and the way potential employees enter and engage with it must change too. Education preparation and workforce placement innovation through the use of learning and employment records is our future. With that, I'm going to start up a little video. Tax cut is one of the most important accomplishments of this Congress, and possibly for generations. It puts money back in the pockets of hardworking Americans and reminds us who we serve: families. But we cannot stop there. We must build on that momentum with a new data paradigm, a partnership of education, industry, and community designed to ensure that every learner and worker has the opportunity to succeed. For students and lifelong learners, this changes everything. Coursework, certifications, apprenticeships, and real-world experiences are all captured in secure digital records. Each skill and competency is verified and portable. No one is reduced to a line on a resume. Every accomplishment is seen, valued, and ready to open doors. For employers, it means clarity and confidence. Real-time labor market data reveals where talent is growing, what wages are trending, and which skills are in demand. Career pathways come into focus, making it easier to recruit, train, and retain the people who drive our economy. Learning and Employment Records, LERs, are the bridge. They connect the learner's proven abilities with the real needs of the workforce. Private, secure, and portable, LERs are powered by technology. Think of it as a transport interstate, an interoperable data highway where information from states, schools, industries, and even federal programs all flow together. The job market becomes more transparent, unlocking opportunities that were once out of reach. For decades, education and workforce data were fragmented and outdated. That was the old paradigm. The new data paradigm replaces it with a universally trusted, public-private system that connects learners, workers, and employers in real time. Opportunity now flows faster, more fairly, and more securely. In Utah, programs like Admit Utah capture this spirit of innovation. Think of an LER like a digital thumb drive you carry in your pocket, except it's captured safely in the cloud. Instead of photos or files, it stores every class you've taken, every certification you've earned, and every skill you've proven. When you apply for a job, you can instantly share that complete, verified record with an employer. No paperwork, no guesswork, just proof of what you can do, ready to plug directly into opportunity, opportunity that will grow with the potential integration of AI, allowing custom tailored services for individuals and real-time data for the labor market. The new data paradigm empowering every American to turn learning into earning. As we shift away from the college-for-all mentality toward a skills-first approach, short-term credentials, work-based learning, and apprenticeships are on the rise. Key legislations like the the enactment of the workforce Pell Grants and the Republicans' recent working families tax cuts will further the growth of these alternative pathways. With over 1 million unique credentials available, pathways options for learners can be very confusing. LERs are here to help solve that problem. We give learners clear insight into the skills needed for their first job and what's needed to continue advancement in their careers. LERs will bring greater clarity to both sides of the labor market, helping workers identify opportunities and employers find the right talent. LERs are the future, but they are not enough on their own. When paired with transparent credential registry and skills-based job descriptions, they can power a talent marketplace where abilities, not pedigrees, drives opportunity. As we modernize our connection of education and work through verifiable credentials, we can build a labor market that works for everyone, where workers have the agency, employees have confidence, and opportunities based on what you know and what you can do day one. With that, I'd like to yield to the ranking member.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and thank you to our witnesses for joining us today. Right now, many of my constituents are facing the reality that the economy is not working for them. Costs are rising, opportunities are disappearing. Since President Trump returned to office in January, job growth has slowed to a crawl, averaging just 70,000 per month compared to the 336,000 per month during the Biden administration. And to make matters worse, the Trump administration continues to fire thousands of public servants without cause, putting them out of work and unable to provide for themselves and their families. As unemployment rises, many job seekers are looking to advance their skills to open the door to a new kind of work. Today's hearing will focus on learning and employment records, or LERs, which the Brookings Institution defines as a comprehensive digital record of interconnected data, such as employment, earnings, skills, and credentials. LERs would provide each person in the workforce with a portfolio containing digital, verifiable records of their past work experience, accumulated skills, competencies, credentials, college transcripts, and other relevant information that they could send to employers instead of a traditional resume. LERs have the potential to make our economy more efficient, more equitable, and more productive. Employers are becoming overwhelmed with job applications containing limited information about the candidates' skills, all of which can be hard to verify. Far too many employers have fallen into the habit of requiring college degrees for jobs that do not necessarily require them, effectively shutting out talented and qualified individuals who have the skills, but not the diploma. But employers in our economy are losing out on the roughly 2/3 of talented, working-age Americans who do not hold a four-year degree. Requiring a college degree contributes to economic disparities, particularly for people who face systemic barriers to completing higher education, which were made by student loan caps included in the big, ugly bill. Some employers are increasingly evaluating job applicants based on experience and skills assessments rather than formal credentials or degrees. Many major companies, such as Google, Apple, IBM, have implemented skills-based hiring practices to bolster their workforces. These examples show that, when implemented well, learning and employment records have the potential to provide employers with skilled workers and provide job seekers with the tools to land a good-paying job to earn a living for themselves and their families. But while the potential is great, so are the challenges. First, our current job market lacks the level of technological infrastructure to support widespread adoption of these practices. And while efforts are underway in some states to digitize credentials and develop learning and employment records, these efforts are hampered by low awareness, lack of common data definitions and standards, lack of digital literacy and access, and data privacy concerns. Additionally, learning and employment records must be equitable and provide opportunities for all job seekers and employers. So, we must ensure that a shift to learning and employment records does not enable an infringement on worker rights, on increased discrimination, or widen achievement and income gaps. To avoid this, we should make sure that learning and employment records are wholly owned and controlled by workers themselves so that they are the ones making key decisions about what kind of information is inputted into their LERs, what information can be open to verification, and what information can or cannot be shared with outside entities. These protections will give workers control over important data privacy elements, such as demographic information, and ensure that unethical employers can't upload false or denigrating information about an employee, which could be done as a retaliatory tactic. Additionally, for LERs to be scaled up, we should make sure that the data definitions and protocols that allow LERs to be dynamically linked with other databases and workforce actors are open-sourced. While employers are leading the way on informing the public about the utility of LERs, we should not become too reliant on proprietary data systems where LERs are incapable of communicating to the wider workforce system. I am encouraged by the bipartisan enthusiasm for LERs today, Mr. Chairman, and I look forward to discussing how these new technologies can expand opportunities for all Americans and how we can best utilize them to connect skilled workers with promising careers. Mr. Chairman, I look forward to our discussion today. I thank you, and I yield back the balance of my time.

Thank you. Thank you very much. And without objection, the hearing record will remain open for 14 days to allow such statements and other materials noted during the hearing to be submitted for the official hearing record. I'll now turn to the introduction of our four distinguished witnesses. Our first witness is Scott Pulsipher, the president of Western Governors University in the great state of Utah. The second witness is Mr. Greg DiDonato, the Vice President of Business Development in EBSCO Information Services here in Washington, D.C. The third witness is Mr. Scott Cheney, the Chief Executive Officer for Credential Engine here in Washington, D.C. And the fourth witness is Mr. Alex Kaplan, an advisor at the American Association of College Registrars and Administrators— Administration Officers from Orange County, California. We thank the witnesses for being here today and look forward to your testimony. Pursuant to committee rules, I would ask each of you to limit your oral presentation to a 3-minute summary of your written statement. As committee members have many questions for you, the clock will count down from 3 minutes. However, pursuant to committee rule 8(d) and committee practice, committee practice will not cut you off from your testimony until you reach your 5-minute mark. I also like to remind the witnesses to be aware of the responsibility to provide accurate information to the subcommittee. I will first recognize Mr. Pulsipher for your testimony.

Thank you, Chairman Owens and Ranking Member Adams. It's a pleasure to be here. Thank you, members of the subcommittee. Thank you for the opportunity to share my perspective on the value of learning and employment records. My name is Scott Pulsipher, and I've nearly for 10 years served as the president of Western Governors University. WGU is a private, nonprofit institution founded in 1997 by a bipartisan group of 19 governors who saw the opportunity to leverage technology and competency-based education to improve access, quality, and outcomes in higher education. Today, we graduate more than 60,000 students annually and have an alumni network of over 410,000 whose lives and careers reflect the promise of opportunity. At WGU, we believe that education must be designed to benefit individuals first, first and foremost, by connecting them with opportunity. After all, when individuals thrive, workforce strength, economic vitality, and innovation follow. That same belief guides our work on LERs. While LERs create value in many ways, their primary purpose is a tool for empowering individuals. As such, our LER at WGU is designed to give individuals greater control over their educational and career pathways. A comprehensive, verified record of skills earned across a lifetime allows people to understand what they can do, where they can go, and what they need to learn next. It lets job seekers apply for roles with skills-rich credentials, clearly communicate their strengths, and share proof of their capabilities down to an atomic level. As AI reshapes roles at an unprecedented speed, the need for real-time, granular skill signaling mechanisms is greater than ever. LERs meet this need by allowing students to share verified skill data throughout their learning journey, not just at graduation. More than just a tool to connect with employers, WGU's LER platform is designed to be used as soon as students begin their educational journey, helping them to understand their current their current skill profile, discover career pathways, and follow a personalized roadmap toward their desired profession. In this way, LERs unlock powerful pathfinding tools, allowing students to explore without drifting aimlessly and racking up student debt in the process. In short, LERs shift agency to the individual and enable career mobility based on proven ability, not pedigree. When readiness is signaled through verified skill, opportunity expands to include those who might otherwise have been overlooked, strengthening organizations and communities. Few things are more profoundly human than enabling individuals to pursue a self-determined life. LERs, while seemingly abstract, exist for that purpose. They translate what individuals know and can do into real opportunity. Our challenge today is not a deficit of talent, but a failure in how we identify, signal, and engage it. Skills-rich LERs contribute to changing that by making talent visible, portable, and actionable. Thank you for the opportunity to testify before you today, and I look forward to your questions.
Thank you. I will now recognize Mr. DiDonato for your testimony.

Chairman Owens, Ranking Member Adams, and distinguished members of the subcommittee, thank you for the opportunity to testify before you today. My name is Greg DiDonato, Vice President of Business Development at EBSCOed. Our mission is simple: to make all learning count by connecting talented Americans with opportunities and employers through the common denominator of skills. Today, I want to share what has been achieved with the Alabama Talent Triad, the nation's first fully operational statewide talent marketplace, as well as convey why this model matters for modernizing our education and workforce system nationally. Alabama launched the Talent Triad statewide in 2024 as a population-level solution to support all students and job seekers, employers and industries, and education training providers. In just 14 months, Alabama has implemented the infrastructure for a skills-based economy that connects the supply and demand sides of the labor market. More than 132,000 Alabamians now have validated LERs. 19,000 credentials in the state have been translated into competencies and are made transparent through the Alabama Credential Registry. Over 300 employers have engaged, and up to 10,000 jobs have been available at any given time. LERs give every learner, from 8th grade to career changers to veterans, a verified, portable record of their skills and credentials. The Credential Registry brings transparency and accountability, documenting and issuing the skills programs teach and the credentials that validate the mastery required by employers. Skills-based job descriptions help employers signal their needs more clearly and connect a more qualified talent pool. Together, these tools create signaling mechanisms and real-time feedback loops between the supply and demand sides of our economy. Students see which programs lead to good jobs, employers see which programs meet industry needs, policymakers see outcomes in real times. These insights lead to shifts in paradigm program design, hiring practices, and yield new and innovative approaches for Americans to transform, transcribe, and transact skills in an ever-changing labor market. Scaling statewide and regional talent marketplaces supports the implementation of Workforce Pell. Credential quality and transparency processes allow states to evaluate short-term credentials and associated programs for quality outcomes and alignment with employer demand. The same process ensures transparency and accountability of learning outcomes, and education training programs can now be documented in terms of competencies that are matched to employers' job descriptions. Talent marketplaces also address workforce shortages and help to increase the labor force participation rate by assisting 43 million Americans with some college, no degree, veterans, disconnected youth, mid-career workers, and all Americans, allow all Americans to prepare for technological change and increase their resilience in the face of ever-changing labor market conditions. The bottom line: unified talent marketplaces and LERs work for all Americans, all career paths, and all industries. They create clearer pathways to good jobs and help employers find the talent they need. That's why EBSCOed has released a free national LER at ler.me to jumpstart this innovative work across all states. Thank you for your time and your continued bipartisan leadership in strengthening America's workforce. EBSCOed stands ready to support this work as we strive to ensure every American can connect their learning to opportunity.
Thank you so much. And I'd like to recognize Mr. Cheney for your testimony.

Thank you. Chairman Owens, Ranking Member Adams, Chairman Walberg, and Ranking Member Scott, and members of the subcommittee, I'm pleased to join this distinguished panel today. Just yesterday, we released the latest Counting Credentials report, in which we reveal that there are at least 1.85 million unique credentials available in the US alone. These include badges, certificates, certifications, licenses, degrees of all types and all levels, and they're offered by more than 134,000 different providers or entities, including two- and four-year institutions, licensing and industry certification bodies, and private companies. One of the significant findings in this report is that more and more credentials are being issued in digital formats. When credential and skill information exists digitally, they become searchable, verifiable, and interoperable, including through digital wallets and LERs. A paper certificate can hang on a wall. A digital certificate or credential can populate a job application, unlock a learning pathway, or be discovered by an employer searching for someone with specific skills. Two takeaways from this report: First, everybody needs help making sense of and navigating this very confusing landscape. And second, we're close to a point where we can both capture all learning through digital credentials, and we can curate all credentials and skills a person has earned in digital records such as LERs. To make this possible, here are four areas that I believe require governmental action. First, ensure that the value of digital credentials, skills, and LERs reach everybody across all education and income levels, and in all communities. You can require that all relevant state and local plans under places like WIOA, Perkins V, ESSA, and the comprehensive economic development plans include planning for supporting, funding, and procuring LERs, as well as enforcing data privacy and security. Requiring that LER planning occurs across education, workforce, and economic development will increase their adoption, use, and value. Second, require the use of open and interoperable data standards. Congress should require that information about all providers, programs, credentials, and skills across all federally funded and authorized programs be made publicly available through open and interoperable data, for which the Credential Transparency Description Language is the de facto standard. Open data requirements must also extend across employment data as well, so that LERs can live up to their name by holding records of an individual's full learning and employment history. And in fact, no federal funding should be used on LERs that do not meet standards for open and interoperable data. Third, extend existing data privacy and security laws and protections to cover LERs as well. And fourth, the true value of an LER comes from validated records of credential and skill attainment, but validating skills is still a major challenge. Congress should include in both legislation and appropriations targeted support to improve the ability to validate skills attainment quickly, efficiently, accurately, and at scale. I look forward to answering any questions you may have. Thank you.
Thank you. And like, Dr.—lastly, recognize Mr. Kaplan for your testimony.

Thank you, Chairman, Ranking Member, and members of the subcommittee, and thank you for the opportunity to testify. My name is Alex Kaplan. I'm an independent expert on learning and employer— learning and records and an advisor to the American Association of Collegiate Registrars and Admissions Officers on artificial intelligence and LERs. Seven years ago, while serving on the American Workforce Policy Advisory Board as part of the IBM team, I spoke at the White House about a vision for how a secure, verifiable, lifelong digital record of learning can help people connect with good jobs. Today, that vision—learning and employment records, or LERs—is within reach. Why this matters is simple. Tens of millions of Americans have built skills through diverse life experiences, but those hard-earned skills remain invisible to most employers. Skills earned through alternative routes are often overlooked, impeding job hunts and career prospects. As verified, portable, skills-rich credentials, LERs show what a person can actually do, regardless of where they learned it. For workers, this improves job and career options. For employers, LERs expand talent pools to candidates they might otherwise overlook and speed up hiring, making it cheaper and more efficient. Artificial intelligence makes LERs even more urgent. AI is creating a crisis of trust in hiring. Neither employers nor job seekers trust each other's authenticity. At the same time, AI can enable precise skills matching if it has verified data to work with. And AI is accelerating skill obsolescence, making dynamic records of current capabilities more valuable than static degrees. LERs provide the verified data infrastructure AI systems need. The momentum behind LERs is real. States like Alabama, Arkansas, Kentucky, and California are building statewide LER ecosystems as workforce development infrastructure. Employers are beginning to adopt skills-based hiring, with early success in using verified credentials to speed background checks. LERs are no longer theoretical. They are here. LERs are not without their challenges. Key amongst them are ensuring robust verification to prevent credential fraud and engineering learner control of LER data into the national system. We are aware of these challenges and understand how to address them. Lastly, due to the hard work of many people and organizations, the technical foundation for a national LER infrastructure has been established and is being tested in multiple states. As federal leadership is essential to scaling a national LER infrastructure, I offer some suggestions on how to proceed. First, lead by example in the use of LERs for federal hiring. Second, convene organizations who have led LER development over the past seven years to advise on the path forward. Third, invest in a decentralized and interoperable national LER infrastructure. Fourth, enable adoption by removing barriers to the use and issuance of LERs. Fifth, encourage private sector entrepreneurship, innovation, and participation in the LER journey. With your leadership, we can ensure that every American's skills, however and wherever earned, are visible, verified, and valued. Thank you.

Thank you. Under Committee Rule 9, we will now question witnesses under the five-minute rule. I will recognize myself for five minutes. Mr. Pulsipher, WGU has been at the forefront of LERs. And I want to thank you, by the way, for your participation at the very first Trump term to kind of get this process started. Can you tell us more about why WGU felt the need to lead on this?

Yeah, thank you, Chairman, for that question. I think it's pretty simple that WGU believes that education has to be a pathway to opportunity. And so one of the core elements of that is ensuring that the individuals that have now acquired a credential and all the competencies and skills associated with that can appropriately communicate that into the world of work. Because one of the key challenges is that every individual through that education wants to ensure that they're readied with the knowledge, skill, and ability necessary for the job. In providing now individuals, the graduates and students at WGU, with that digital transcript that has the verified skills in it, the employers now, or the workforce now, in fact, have a very clear articulation of what our graduates are readied to do. So it better aligns with the skills, the tasks, activities that exist in roles, and so that those employers can actually ensure that our graduates are skilled and credible. The other key thing is, is that it does increase the ability for those individuals to personally navigate the career options that they have in a geolocated way. Meaning that specifically with our achievement wallet, our LER, it now surfaces to them the roles at which employers in their specific location that they already have the skills that would ready for them for those jobs, and it even automates the way and mechanisms by which they can apply for those jobs and surface their transcripts, these LERs, to those employers.
Okay, thank you so much. Mr. DiDonato, what are the more important lessons learned from the early pilots that we should understand?

Thank you for the question. I would say there's several lessons that that we've learned through this implementation in Alabama as well as some other pilots that we've been a part of. Number one, messaging. Talent marketplaces can mean a lot of different things to a lot of different people, so we need to really make sure that we have very specific messaging, clear messaging, easy-to-understand messaging for each of the user personas, whether it's students, whether it's veterans, education and training providers, employers, etc., about what this means to them and how this is supportive. Two, partnerships are extremely important. There's a lot of really good work happening at each level, but in siloed work, and so we need to make sure that talent marketplaces and LERs are an amplification of what's happening as opposed to it being a threatening existence to them. So partnerships are extremely important all the way across the board. Without them, obviously, this work does not exist. Legislation and funding. Time is of essence to a lot of folks. The folks who are invested in this, whether it's employers, whether it's education, training providers, whether it's students, whether it's job seekers, need to know that this is going to be a persistent opportunity for them to invest their time that that's needed. So, funding, legislation, the signals that they know that this opportunity will last for the long haul is important. It's an evolving conversation, so we need to make sure that the technologies we're utilizing, what we're investing in, also we're evolving and consistently moving at a rapid speed and have those capabilities. And then lastly, we need big data. We need a lot of information to make this work. We need a lot of information to make sure we're understanding the cross-sectoral partnerships and opportunities that are out there. I would say those are all key lessons that we've learned throughout this process.

Thank you. Mr. Kaplan, you and other witnesses have highlighted that LERs are a tool that fits within the broader framework of a talent marketplace. How could this be— how could this kind of tool facilitate better coordination across different systems?

Thank you for that question. The thing about learning and employment records is that they represent a common set of data and a common set of protocols around the skills and competency that individuals have accumulated over the course of their lifetime. If we can settle on this common set of standards, which we're well on our way to doing, we'll be able to enable people to transfer those— that information about themselves from one place to another. To employers, to academic institutions, and for those employers and institutions and others to see that that verifiable data is accurate and correct, enabling them to do things like offer a job to somebody, admit them to their university. So there are a lot of opportunities here where by bringing LERs to the forefront and establishing them as a common set of data, we'll be able to use them in order to support and make easier the navigation of the talent marketplace.
Thank you. I now recognize the ranking member for purpose of questioning the witnesses.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Again, thank you, gentlemen, for being here. From 2021 to 2025, Credential Engine partnered with with eight community colleges in North Carolina as part of their Aligning the Workforce Education System for Manufacturing. This is a project which was funded by the Department of Labor through a Strengthening Community Colleges Training Grant. Mr. Cheney, could you tell me more about Credential Engine's work on on this project, particularly related to competency-based digital badging? And given the success of the project, what role can WIOA-funded programs play in standardizing credentials?

Yes, thank you for that question. So, yeah, Forsyth was a pretty tremendous leader in this project. They convened a number of regional community colleges so that they could collectively work on a manufacturing initiative along with a dozen or more manufacturing companies. And what they recognized was that this was a regional initiative, that there were many players in it, it wasn't just Forsyth. And so what we were doing there is putting all of the information—you've heard the conversation this morning about open data and interoperable data—so we were working with Forsyth and the other community colleges to make available information about the credentials that they offer, the programs, the competencies, and skills into this open, interoperable data format so they could be used both in translating what students had earned and what they knew to the employers that were in the manufacturing sector in that region. And they could use it also to move between the colleges and not be locked into just one program, but they could get the training and skills they needed more easily across the different colleges.

Okay, thank you, sir. In your testimony, you mentioned that worker protection should be included with any effort to increase the use of LER, specifically employer surveillance, retaliation— retaliation as a concern. For example, an employee could refuse— employer could refuse to validate a worker's credentials as a form of retaliation. And so as these LEAs become more common, what guardrails can the federal government implement to prevent employers from using them as a mechanism to retaliate against workers?

So I would say the, the most important thing is to ensure that the information about what an individual has earned is actually in their control. So it's quite likely that an employer or an employee will earn credentials both through the employer but also outside. So regardless of where they earn it, that information should be securely included in an LER so that employer or that employee has control over it.
Okay, so, uh-huh,
no, that's fine.

So, so in your testimony, uh, you state that the data rights and privacy must be foundational in an implementation of LERs and that workers should own and completely control their LERs, including the data and the information that make up, make up the LER and what can and cannot be shared with employers. So can you elaborate on the risks of scaling up the use of LERs without ensuring that workers retain ownership or control?

I would say that the, the risks are the same if we're talking about just education data or any personally identifiable information. LERs are just another example of where we're helping to make information about what someone has earned accessible for their control. So as I pointed out in my testimony, I think one of the things we need to do is to just extend the existing privacy and data security laws we have on the books so that they cover LERs as well.

Okay. Now, according to recent surveys, many employers say they struggle to evaluate the return on investments for training programs. So could LERs make— help measure training effectiveness and workforce readiness more accurately?

So there's a number of issues that are at play there. They can certainly help because we'll have in one place a more secure and more accurate record of what an individual has earned and where they've earned it. Right now, we try and come up with impact information about short-term credentials, which is very, very difficult. We're making some good progress on that, of being able to get better outcome data for short-term credentials, but having it all in a secure record would make it easier to evaluate what an individual has earned and and how effective it's been.
Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. I'll yield back my 13 seconds.
Thank you so much. I'd now like to recognize the chairman of the full committee, my friend from Michigan, Chairman Walberg.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, and thank you as well for that amazing video. Second time I've seen that, but I've—as I've told you, I still refuse to believe that you're the graphic artist until I see the Super Bowl ring on that hand, okay? Mr. Pulsipher, good to see you again. Who are the key stakeholders in the education space that are the most important partners when it comes to scaling LERs?

Yeah, thank you for that question, Chairman. I think you have to start with institutions themselves. I mean, educational institutions, they are key stakeholders because effectively they're the ones who in fact are verifying or validating the the skills and competencies that individuals are acquiring, including the credentials that they're awarded as a result of that. If they are not moving towards more of a digital transcript of those skills and competencies, then in fact the talent economy or that talent marketplace fails. You certainly see the employers as key stakeholders as well. They have to be able to ingest this machine-readable digital transcript of those skills rather than calling into an institution to validate that they actually graduated from that, have the degree, etc. But you also have technology companies and the, uh, those providers of that data set, whether it's applicant tracking system, HRIS— HRIS meaning human resource information systems, etc.— they are also key stakeholders. But all of those are there ultimately to support the individual as the primary stakeholder. The individual ultimately has to see the value in its signaling being a better signal of the capabilities that they have that are relevant to the jobs that they're seeking.
And that certainly is key with all of education, isn't it?
It is.

Yeah, that individual. Thank you. Mr. DiDonato, how do LERs and the system they're part of actually use AI to create the matches between programs, credentials, and job descriptions that you've described?

Thank you, sir, for the question. Um, we make sure that the AI is trained on validated data, verifiable data, and good data. The AI today is— there's a chance that AI ultimately is utilizing inappropriate data that's just obscured and ineffective. We're making sure that the validated data, that you're getting from student records, from employers, from the education training providers is, is what's training the AI. So the AI works for us instead of us working for the AI.
Have that human moral factual thumbprint, right?
Yes, we have a human in a loop to make sure that it is working appropriately.

Okay Thank you. Mr. Kaplan, we've heard about some of the LER pilots that have been adopted around the country. Could you speak about the importance of interoperability as tools like LERs are developed?

Yes, thank you for the question. So interoperability is essential to the functioning of a national learning and employment record infrastructure. The reason for that is because people move. They move around, they go from state to state, and they look for jobs all over the country. So we need to enable a credential that's issued in Alabama to be accepted by an academic institution or an employer in California. Absent interoperability, we're going to see the rise of, I'll call, walled gardens of data that really impede the ability of individuals to use that data and to make that data essential to their job hunts and their career explorations.
Thank you. I appreciate the, the answers, and, uh, I yield back 1 minute and 12 seconds.
Thank you, Mr. Chair. Appreciate it. I'd like to now recognize my friend from Georgia, Ms. McBath.

Thank you, Chairman, and thank you, gentlemen, for being here this morning. Really appreciate you, and I'm so glad this is such a bipartisan issue for our committee. We're excited about that. Mr. Pulsipher, good to see you again, and Mr. Cheney. I know that you are both fully committed to ensuring that every American is able to easily navigate and understand the continuously expanding universe of degrees, credentials, and competencies. I deeply appreciate your input, as well as the other witnesses, for joining us for today's discussion on learning and employment records, or as we're calling them, LERs. The American people are angry, and that anger is truly justified.
